module: Mark synthetic outputs and verify detection

lesson.title: Synthetic outputs: marks, labels and detection
lesson.summary: Recognise synthetic content and distinguish machine-readable marks, human labels and detection.

prerequisites.reason: The learner must recognise the regulated system before applying this rule.
The learner must identify the actor responsible for design and output marking.
The learner must preserve other applicable duties when applying this transparency rule.

blocks: **Synthetic content** is content artificially generated or manipulated by an AI system. Article 50(2) addresses audio, images, video and text, including outputs of general-purpose AI systems.
Harbour's system generates a voice clip and a text answer. Both need the paragraph 2 analysis. Realism, public publication or a deceptive purpose is not a universal condition of this provider duty.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 50(2), 50(4)-(5); Guidelines paragraphs 55-77
Commission Article 50 Guidelines C(2026) 5054 final; non-binding interpretation
Final Transparency Code, 10 June 2026; voluntary implementation framework

blocks: **Machine-readable marking** embeds or attaches information that a machine can use to recognise artificial generation or manipulation. A **visible disclosure** tells people about AI involvement in a way they can perceive.

These serve different duties. A visible 'AI' badge alone does not necessarily provide a machine-readable marker and a detection route. A hidden machine-readable marker alone does not necessarily give the person the required disclosure.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 50(2), 50(4)-(5); Guidelines paragraphs 55-77
Commission Article 50 Guidelines C(2026) 5054 final; non-binding interpretation
Final Transparency Code, 10 June 2026; voluntary implementation framework

blocks: A **detection mechanism** reads or verifies the relevant marking. Pair the marker with a route capable of identifying it. A signed metadata record can have a verifier; a watermark needs a compatible detector.

Metadata is information attached to a file. A digital signature helps verify its origin and integrity. A watermark places a marker within the content itself. Later lessons examine their different limits.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 50(2), 50(4)-(5); Guidelines paragraphs 55-77
Commission Article 50 Guidelines C(2026) 5054 final; non-binding interpretation
Final Transparency Code, 10 June 2026; voluntary implementation framework

blocks: The Code's provider section addresses access to detection, readable results and privacy/security protections. For example, detection of metadata and public detection of non-free-form-text watermarks are generally offered free; specific exceptions and access conditions must be checked in Measure 2.1.

For upload-based detection, Code Sub-measure 2.1.3 addresses confidentiality, minimisation and deletion of uploaded content immediately after detection; limited minimal security/abuse logs have distinct conditions. A verbatim copy is not retained. An AI-detection website guessing from style is not automatically a detector for the provider's marker. Such forensic detection examines characteristics without requiring a prior mark; it can err and is not the same evidence.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 50(2), 50(4)-(5); Guidelines paragraphs 55-77

Final Transparency Code, 10 June 2026; voluntary implementation framework

blocks: A detection result should explain what was detected clearly and accessibly. It does not certify that the content is accurate, lawful or harmless.

In Harbour's review, first identify the paragraph 2 output, then its marker, its detection route and what the result actually establishes. Preserve the separate deployer disclosure analysis for later use.

options.reason: This provider duty is distinct from the public-interest publication rule.
